The '95%' saying is attributed to Gerald Zaltman; a market-research firm's blog and a business magazine describe it as his estimate from an interview or book of about 2003, with no study behind it.

sources.citation: Poldrack, R. A. (2006). Can cognitive processes be inferred from neuroimaging data? Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 10(2), 59-63.
Yarkoni, T. (2011). The New York Times blows it big time on brain imaging (blog post on the Lindstrom opinion piece).
Poldrack, R. A. (2011). Signers of letter to the editor of the New York Times (blog post).
Ariely, D., & Berns, G. S. (2010). Neuromarketing: The hope and hype of neuroimaging in business. Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 11(4), 284-292.

Venkatraman, V., Dimoka, A., Pavlou, P. A., et al. (2015). Predicting advertising success beyond traditional measures: New insights from neurophysiological methods and market response modeling. Journal of Marketing Research, 52(4), 436-452.
Scholte, H. S., van der Leij, A., & Lamme, V. A. F. (2022). [Vendor-affiliated paper that summarises the 2015 study's figures; title not confirmed].
Inc. magazine. Harvard Professor Says 95% of Purchasing Decisions Are Subconscious.

entries.caveats: The 2015 study does show that brain scans can carry information that questionnaires miss, so the field is not empty. Eye tracking used to see where people look is a sound method with its own limits (see heat-map-limits); the criticism here concerns eye tracking sold as a measure of emotion or intention.

entries.principle: A typeface that fits the product is chosen more often than one that does not
entries.claim: When people chose between two brands of the same product, they chose the brand set in a typeface judged appropriate for that product about twice as often as the brand set in an inappropriate typeface, across ten product categories. In a small field test, people took chocolates from the box with the appropriate typeface three times out of four. Fit depends on how well the feeling of the typeface (how strong and how lively it seems) matches the feeling of the product.
entries.mechanism: A typeface carries associations before a word is read: heavy or light, formal or playful, old or new. When those associations match what the reader expects of the product, the name is processed with less friction and the brand seems more believable. A mismatch makes the reader hesitate.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — slightly; a fitting typeface does not have to be explained away
effects.satisfaction: raises — fitting typefaces were chosen more often in the experiments
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the look matches what the visitor expects from this kind of business

designMoves: Write down three tone words for the business before choosing a typeface, and choose a typeface whose character matches them.
Test the business name in two or three candidate typefaces with a few members of the audience.
Apply the expressive typeface to the name and the headings; keep body text in a typeface chosen for legibility.
antiPatterns: A playful rounded display typeface for a law firm, or a severe condensed one for a nursery, with no intent behind the contrast.
Choosing a typeface because it is fashionable, with no thought for the product.
The claim that one typeface (for example Baskerville) makes statements more believable, taken as a rule.

howToCheck.machine: A program cannot derive the character of a typeface from its file. The Catalog must hold character tags for each typeface it offers (for example 'formal', 'warm', 'technical', 'playful'). Report the heading and body typefaces of the page and compare the heading typeface's tags with the tone words in the Prescription; flag a heading typeface that shares no tag with them.
howToCheck.human: Show the business name in the chosen typeface to five people and ask which of three kinds of business it belongs to. More than chance (one in three) should name the right kind.

evidence.strengthNote: All sources were seen only as search summaries. Doyle and Bottomley (2004, Journal of Business Research): forced choices in 10 product categories; brands in an appropriate typeface were chosen about twice as often, even when the brand names carried strong meaning of their own; in a small field study people chose chocolates from the box with the appropriate typeface 75% of the time. Doyle and Bottomley (2006, Journal of Consumer Psychology): judged appropriateness depends partly on the match between typeface and product on perceived strength and activity. Henderson, Giese and Cote (2004, Journal of Marketing): the design of typefaces reduces to six dimensions (elaborate, harmony, natural, flourish, weight, compressed) that shape the impressions people form; the number of typefaces studied (remembered as 210) was not confirmed. All are laboratory choices and ratings of brand names, not of websites, and sample sizes were not confirmed. The Baskerville claim comes from a 2012 newspaper experiment by Errol Morris: readers saw a statement in one of six typefaces and Baskerville drew slightly more agreement; the size of the sample (remembered as about 45,000) and of the effect (remembered as about 1.5 percentage points) were not confirmed, and a secondary blog gives the lead over the next typeface as 5 in 1,000. It was not peer-reviewed.

sources.citation: Doyle, J. R., & Bottomley, P. A. (2004). Font appropriateness and brand choice. Journal of Business Research, 57(8), 873-880.
Doyle, J. R., & Bottomley, P. A. (2006). Dressed for the occasion: Font-product congruity in the perception of logotype. Journal of Consumer Psychology, 16(2), 112-123.
Henderson, P. W., Giese, J. L., & Cote, J. A. (2004). Impression management using typeface design. Journal of Marketing, 68(4), 60-72.
Morris, E. (2012). Hear, All Ye People; Hearken, O Earth (two-part article on the Baskerville experiment). The New York Times.

entries.caveats: The existing records personality-vs-legibility and typography-mood-and-impression show that typefaces have personalities and affect mood; this record adds the effect on choice. Associations shift with culture and fashion. A deliberate mismatch can work as a signature when the rest of the design supports it.

entries.principle: Rounded letterforms and logos read as soft, sweet and warm; angular ones as hard, sharp and durable; a link to trust is not established
entries.claim: People match rounded typefaces with the word 'sweet' and angular typefaces with 'sour', 'bitter' and 'salty', and they like rounded typefaces more and judge them easier to read. A circular logo made a shoe seem more comfortable and a company seem more caring; an angular logo made the same shoe seem more durable. No study was found that shows that a rounded typeface raises trust.
entries.mechanism: People carry associations from touch and taste over to sight: round things are soft and safe to handle, angular things are hard and can cut. The shape of letters and logos borrows these meanings. The associations describe what a brand seems to be like (gentle or tough), which is different from whether people believe it.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — no measured effect on reading performance; rounded faces were only judged easier to read
effects.satisfaction: raises — slightly; rounded typefaces were liked more in one study
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: none — no evidence

designMoves: Use rounded letterforms, logos and corners together when the business should seem gentle, friendly or comforting: childcare, bakery, wellness.
Use angular or sharp-cornered forms when the business should seem precise, strong or durable: tools, engineering, security.
Keep the shape language the same across typeface, logo and corner radius, so that the signals do not cancel out.
Earn trust by other means: clear contact details, real photographs, no errors (see the existing records on trust).
antiPatterns: Rounded typeface, sharp logo and square buttons mixed without intent.
The claim that rounded typefaces make a site more trustworthy.
A very soft look for a business whose customers want proof of strength, or the reverse.

howToCheck.machine: The Catalog tags each typeface it offers as 'rounded', 'neutral' or 'angular'. Read the heading typeface's tag and the dominant corner class of buttons and cards (angular, moderate, pill). Flag a rounded typeface combined with 'precise', 'durable', 'technical' or 'strong' in the Prescription's tone words, and an angular one combined with 'warm', 'gentle', 'friendly' or 'comforting'. Flag a rounded typeface with fully angular corners, or the reverse, as an inconsistency to confirm. No measurable check for trust exists.
howToCheck.human: Ask three people whether the page feels soft or hard, and whether that suits the business.

evidence.strengthNote: All sources were seen only as search summaries. Velasco, Woods, Hyndman and Spence (2015, i-Perception): twelve typefaces from round to angular (two versions of Arial and ten drawn for the study); rounder typefaces were matched with 'sweet' and angular ones with 'bitter', 'salty' and 'sour'; a second experiment found that rounder typefaces were liked more and judged easier to read; these are ratings, and reading speed was not measured. Jiang, Gorn, Galli and Chattopadhyay (2016, Journal of Consumer Research): a circular logo raised rated comfort and an angular logo raised rated durability of the same shoe, and a round logo made a company seem more caring, warm and sensitive to customers; the effect held when participants memorised a number at the same time. Zhuo and colleagues (2025): rounded corners in an app raised rated warmth. On trust the search found only shape studies outside typography: a review of product design states that rounded forms express warmth, which includes seeming friendly and trustworthy, while one draft study of medical devices found no effect of angularity on rated trust. Grade A- applies to the soft-hard association; the trust claim is grade C at best.

sources.citation: Velasco, C., Woods, A. T., Hyndman, S., & Spence, C. (2015). The taste of typeface. i-Perception, 6(4).

Jiang, Y., Gorn, G. J., Galli, M., & Chattopadhyay, A. (2016). Does your company have the right logo? How and why circular- and angular-logo shapes influence brand attribute judgments. Journal of Consumer Research, 42(5), 709-726.
Zhuo, S., et al. (2025). How a rounded aesthetic translates beauty to function and prosociality: The persuasive effects of warmth. Journal of User Experience, 20(3).
[Authors not confirmed] (2021). [Review of angular and rounded shapes, warmth and competence in product design]. Frontiers in Psychology, 12, 615647.

entries.caveats: One of the authors of the typeface study designed ten of its typefaces. Taste words are a laboratory way to reveal associations; nobody tastes a website. The associations were measured in a few countries.

entries.principle: A dark theme is a comfort and preference option; for most people it reads no better than a light theme, and worse for small text and in dark rooms
entries.claim: Polarity is the relation of text to background: positive polarity is dark text on a light background, negative polarity is light text on a dark background. For glance-reading of single words, negative polarity in near-darkness gave the worst legibility of all combinations tested; positive polarity in near-darkness and both polarities in daylight-like lighting were significantly better. The advantage of positive polarity is largest for small characters. Some people with clouded lenses, as in cataract, are reported to read better with negative polarity. Data on how many people prefer a dark theme are weak: a poll of 115 phone users found about a third using dark, a third light and a third both.
entries.mechanism: A bright screen makes the pupil smaller. A smaller pupil gives a sharper image on the retina, as a small aperture does in a camera, so fine detail is easier to see. A dark screen in a dark room leaves the pupil wide, and the image is blurrier. In an eye with a clouded lens, the light of a bright background scatters inside the eye and washes out the letters, so a dark background can help.

effects.cognitiveLoad: raises — slightly, for small text in a dark theme and for people with normal vision
effects.satisfaction: raises — for people who prefer a dark theme or find a bright screen glaring in a dark room
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: none — no evidence

designMoves: Make the light theme the default and offer a dark theme that follows the visitor's system setting.
In the dark theme, do not use small or thin text: keep body text at or above the size and weight used in the light theme.
Keep long reading text (terms, articles) comfortable in both themes, and check contrast in both.
Describe the dark theme as a preference and comfort option, not as healthier or easier to read.
antiPatterns: A dark-only site with small, light-weight grey text.
Claims that a dark theme 'reduces eye strain', 'is better for your eyes' or 'is what most users prefer'.
Ignoring the visitor's system setting for light or dark.

howToCheck.machine: Detect polarity from the luminance of body text and background. If the default is negative polarity, flag the absence of a light theme. Emulate prefers-color-scheme light and dark and assert that the page responds when the Prescription asks for two themes. In the dark theme, flag text smaller than the Catalog minimum (for example 16 CSS pixels for body text) or with font-weight below 400, and run the text contrast check (4.5 to 1) in both themes.
howToCheck.human: Read a paragraph of the smallest text in the dark theme in a dim room, on a phone held at normal distance. Then do the same in the light theme in a bright room.

evidence.strengthNote: Grade A- applies to the legibility findings; the preference figures are grade C. All sources were seen only as search summaries. Dobres, Chahine and Reimer (2017, Applied Ergonomics): a word-recognition task that measured the display time needed to read a word, with two type sizes, two polarities and near-dark against daylight-like lighting; the thresholds were highest (worst) for negative polarity in the dark, and positive polarity in the dark and all conditions in bright light were significantly better; the study was aimed at car displays, and whether the two polarities differed from each other in bright light was not confirmed. Piepenbrock, Mayr and Buchner (2014, Ergonomics): smaller pupils and better proofreading with positive polarity; the same authors' 2014 paper in Human Factors is summarised by an index page as showing that negative polarity should be avoided with small type; its abstract was not seen. Low vision: Legge and colleagues (1985) found no effect of polarity for normal vision in their reading studies; the finding that readers with clouded lenses read faster with reversed polarity is remembered from the low-vision paper and was not confirmed by the search. A Nielsen Norman Group review (Budiu, 2020), known through secondary articles and an interview, says that people with conditions such as cataract may do better with a dark theme and that no full agreement exists. Preference: the Nielsen Norman Group poll of 115 phone users (about a third each); a figure that 22% of web traffic in December 2021 came from browsers set to prefer dark, attributed second-hand to a browser maker; a 2024 preprint in which 61.7% of surveyed students preferred dark in learning platforms; a technology website's reader poll with more than 2,500 self-selected respondents. These samples are small or self-selected and disagree. Myopia: Aleman, Wang and Schaeffel (2018, Scientific Reports) found that reading light text on dark thickened a layer of the eye in young adults within about 30 minutes, a short-term stand-in for eye growth; the authors say that the effect on myopia in children remains to be verified.

sources.citation: Dobres, J., Chahine, N., & Reimer, B. (2017). Effects of ambient illumination, contrast polarity, and letter size on text legibility under glance-like reading. Applied Ergonomics, 60, 68-73.
Piepenbrock, C., Mayr, S., & Buchner, A. (2014). Smaller pupil size and better proofreading performance with positive than with negative polarity displays. Ergonomics, 57(11).
Piepenbrock, C., Mayr, S., & Buchner, A. (2014). Positive display polarity is particularly advantageous for small character sizes. Human Factors, 56(5), 942-951.
Legge, G. E., Rubin, G. S., Pelli, D. G., & Schleske, M. M. (1985). Psychophysics of reading II: Low vision. Vision Research, 25, 253-266.
Budiu, R. (2020). Dark Mode vs. Light Mode: Which Is Better? Nielsen Norman Group. (Seen through secondary articles and an interview in Fast Company.)
Nielsen Norman Group. Dark Mode: How Users Think About It and Issues to Avoid. (Title recalled; poll of 115 mobile users.)
[Authors not confirmed] (2024). An exploration of effects of dark mode on university students: A human computer interface analysis. arXiv:2409.10895 (preprint).
Android Authority. Dark mode survey results (reader poll).
Aleman, A. C., Wang, M., & Schaeffel, F. (2018). Reading and myopia: Contrast polarity matters. Scientific Reports, 8, 10840. (Article number recalled.)

entries.caveats: This record extends the existing records light-vs-dark-polarity (the 2013 proofreading study) and folklore-dark-mode-premium. The glance-reading study used single words on a car-style display, not paragraphs on a phone. The 1985 finding of no polarity effect for normal vision differs from the later proofreading findings; the tasks and displays differ. A bright screen in a dark room can be uncomfortable even when it is more legible; comfort and legibility are different outcomes. The search found no evidence for or against the common claim that light text on dark blurs more for people with astigmatism. A dark theme saves energy only on screens whose pixels emit their own light.
